cases.learnTitle: Arterial-phase CT with kidney and renal tumour segmentation
cases.referenceSummary: C4KC-KiTS manual segmentation of the kidneys and of a renal tumour on this arterial-phase series. Other organs and findings are not referenced. The cohort consists of patients who underwent nephrectomy for renal tumours, but the segmentation label is the reference here, not a diagnosis for every structure.
cases.learnNotes: In the arterial (corticomedullary) phase the renal cortex enhances strongly while the medulla is still darker. A mass is recognised by a contour bulge and by enhancement that differs from normal parenchyma. Use coronal MPR to see the kidney's full length.

tasks.title: Was IV contrast given?
tasks.prompt: Look at the aorta and pulmonary arteries in a mediastinal window. Was intravenous contrast given?

options.text: Yes — the vessels are brighter than muscle
options.why: Enhancing vessels are much denser than blood on a non-contrast scan; the DICOM header also records a contrast agent.

options.text: No — blood and muscle look similar
options.why: That describes a non-contrast scan. Measure the aorta with the pixel readout: enhanced blood is well above ~50 HU.

hints.text: Hover the aorta and read the HU value in the bottom-left corner; compare it with the chest wall muscle.

tasks.explanation: Unenhanced blood measures roughly 30–50 HU; with IV contrast the arteries and veins become markedly brighter, depending on timing. Knowing the phase is the first step before calling a vessel abnormal.

tasks.title: Which contrast phase?
tasks.prompt: Look at the aorta and the kidneys. Which contrast phase best describes this series?

options.why: Very bright aorta and a cortex brighter than the medulla — corticomedullary differentiation.
In the portal venous phase the kidneys enhance more uniformly (nephrographic) and the portal vein is bright.
Contrast would be in the collecting systems and ureters.
Vessels would be no brighter than muscle.

hints.text: Compare the renal cortex and medulla: is there a two-tone appearance?

tasks.explanation: Recognising the phase tells you what 'normal' enhancement should look like before you call a lesion. This series is labelled arterial by the source.

tasks.title: Find the kidneys
tasks.prompt: Mark the right kidney and the left kidney with named arrows. Both kidneys form one reference structure here, so each arrow is checked for lying in a kidney; check the side yourself from the edge letters.

hints.text: The kidneys are retroperitoneal, either side of the spine, around L1–L2.
Reveal the reference answer.

tasks.explanation: The source segmentation labels both kidneys as one class, so this task checks localisation; side is checked by your own reading of the edge letters.

tasks.title: Find the renal mass
tasks.prompt: Examine both kidneys through their full length. Mark any focal abnormality you find (point or box), or state that you find none.

hints.text: Follow each kidney's outline slice by slice; look for a bulge or a region whose enhancement differs from the cortex.
Jumping to a slice with the reference.
Reveal the reference answer.

tasks.explanation: A solid renal mass typically distorts the renal contour and enhances differently from the cortex; simple cysts are water density and do not enhance. A box drawn around the mass is also scored for overlap (≥30%) so you can see how well you outlined it. In this patient the upper left kidney also holds a large lesion of near-water density (about 10–20 HU) that the source labels as kidney, not tumour — it behaves like a simple cyst. The scored target is the smaller enhancing solid mass lower in the same kidney; a mark on the cyst is not scored.

rubric.text: Side and pole (upper/inter/lower) of the mass
Enhancement compared with normal cortex; solid vs cystic
Checked renal vein, IVC, nodes and the other kidney

tasks.title: Oral exam: show it, describe it, defend it
tasks.prompt: As if presenting to an examiner: (1) show the key finding with an arrow, (2) describe it in one sentence (location, size, pattern), (3) give your leading interpretation with the image evidence for it, and (4) explain why a complex renal cyst is less likely.

hints.text: Keep it to four sentences. Examiners reward a clear search pattern and an honest statement of what the images cannot tell you (histology needs tissue; one arterial phase limits characterisation).

tasks.explanation: There is no automatic grader for free-text reasoning. Compare your answer with the checklist and the linked book pages.

rubric.text: Showed the finding on the right series and slice
One-sentence description with location, size and pattern
Leading interpretation supported by named image features
Closest alternative (a complex renal cyst) addressed with opposing evidence
Stated what needs comparison, other sequences/phases, or clinical information
